citations.location: Fee Detail sheet, Line 20 (07/08/2024, A. Osei), cell I21
citations.cited_for: Foreseeability framework for consequential damages in Washington commercial contract disputes
citations.context: Research Washington consequential damages law in commercial contract disputes; analyze foreseeability requirements and Hadley v. Baxendale framework; begin drafting research memo.

first_check.correct_citation: Hadley v. Baxendale, 9 Ex. 341, 156 Eng. Rep. 145 (Ex. 1854)
first_check.quote_check: No quotations attributed.
first_check.explanation: Hadley v. Baxendale is a real 1854 Court of Exchequer decision and the foundational foreseeability rule for consequential contract damages: recoverable losses are those arising naturally from the breach or those reasonably in the contemplation of both parties at contracting. Washington courts follow it. The Washington Supreme Court quoted it as 'the general rule as to damages growing out of a breach of contract' in Dally v. Isaacson, 40 Wn.2d 574 (1952), and the Court of Appeals said it 'is still followed in substance in most states, including Washington' and 'lays down a general standard of foreseeability' in King Logging Co. v. Scalzo, 16 Wn. App. 918 (1977). The invoice gives the case name only, with no reporter cite, which is normal for a billing narrative; the full cite is supplied above. The Hadley opinion itself was read only through a WebFetch summary of a course-reader page and through the Washington opinions quoting it, not from the English Reports directly.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: King Logging Co. v. Scalzo: "The rule of Hadley v. Baxendale, supra, governing the recovery of damages for breach of contract is still followed in substance in most states, including Washington". Dally v. Isaacson: "The general rule as to damages growing out of a breach of contract is stated in the early English case, Hadley v. Baxendale (1854), 9 Ex. 341, 354, 156 Eng. Rep. 151, as follows: 'Where two parties have made a contract which one of them has broken, the damages which the other party ought to receive ... should be such as may fairly and reasonably be considered either arising naturally ... or such as may reasonably be supposed to have been in the contemplation of both parties, at the time they made the contract, as the probable result of the breach of it.'"

It contains no privilege log requirement; the phrase "privilege log" does not appear anywhere in the court's posted Local Civil Rules (text search of the full 148-page PDF returned no hits). The nearest content is LCR 26(f)(1)(H), which makes inadvertent-production and FRE 502(d)/(e) privilege-waiver procedures a conference topic, and LCR 26(f)(1)(I)(ii), which points to the court's separate Model ESI Agreement form. (H) procedures for handling inadvertent production of privileged information and other privilege waiver issues pursuant to Rule 502(d) or (e) of the Federal Rules of Evidence;"

second_check.explanation: The first check is right about the rule's own text. In the court's posted Local Civil Rules, LCR 26(f) is the discovery-conference rule, and the only privilege language in it is (1)(H): "procedures for handling inadvertent production of privileged information and other privilege waiver issues pursuant to Rule 502(d) or (e)". The phrase "privilege log" does not appear in it. But the first check stopped short of the Model ESI Agreement, and that is where the privilege-log rules are. LCR 26(f)(1)(I)(ii) makes it a conference topic "whether the parties agree to adopt the Model Agreement Regarding Discovery of Electronically Stored Information ... (the 'Model ESI Agreement' ...)". I read the version dated 2/1/23, which was the one in effect in July 2024. Its Section E ("Privilege") reads: "[The parties should confer regarding the nature and scope of privilege logs for the case ...] 1. A producing party shall create a privilege log of all documents fully withheld from production ... Privilege logs shall include a unique identification number for each document and the basis for the claim ..." It also covers metadata-based logs, deadlines for producing logs, redactions that need not be logged, and an exemption for post-complaint privileged material. So LCR 26(f) leads directly, through the form it names, to the court's standard privilege-log terms. The time entry only describes a research topic. Read fairly, "privilege log requirements under W.D. Wash. LCR 26(f)" is a loose but defensible pointer, not a citation to a rule that has nothing on the subject. The defect is that the operative requirements sit in the Model ESI Agreement, Section E, which LCR 26(f)(1)(I)(ii) incorporates (along with FRCP 26(b)(5)), not in the text of LCR 26(f) itself. That is a minor imprecision, not a mischaracterization.

Entitlement to prejudgment interest is a common-law rule: Hansen v. Rothaus, 107 Wn.2d 468, 472, 730 P.2d 662 (1986).

first_check.explanation: The reference is loose rather than wrong. Washington has statutory interest provisions that courts apply to prejudgment interest: RCW 19.52.010 sets the 12 percent rate (its caption reads "Exception for prejudgment interest"), and Washington appellate courts describe 12 percent under RCW 19.52.010 as "this state's statutory rate" for prejudgment interest. But whether prejudgment interest is available at all is decided by a court-made liquidated-claim rule, not a statute, and the contract/tort distinction the entry mentions appears in the judgment-interest statute, RCW 4.56.110. All Alaskan Seafoods' description of it.
